flashcards.front: What is the primary threat vector for Wireless Network Security?
flashcards.back_definition: Adversaries exploit WPA2 handshake brute-force on router connections to bypass standard perimeter security controls.
flashcards.back_example: Example: AP-WIDS: Deauth flood signature on station MAC
flashcards.back_confusion: Don't confuse this threat with other layers (like physical breaches or certificate revocations) which target different assets.
flashcards.back_hook: Recall: WPA2 handshake brute-force is the unlocked door; router connections is what the attacker wants to steal.

flashcards.front: How does the security team mitigate Wireless Network Security threats?
flashcards.back_definition: Deploying and enforcing WPA3 Enterprise SAE keys directly hardens router connections and blocks unauthorized connections.
flashcards.back_example: Action: Update security configurations to require WPA3 Enterprise SAE keys.
flashcards.back_confusion: Don't confuse mitigation (actively blocking the exploit) with detection (simply logging or alerting the event).
flashcards.back_hook: Mitigation is the shield; detection is the security camera.

flashcards.front: How do analysts detect exploitation of Wireless Network Security?
flashcards.back_definition: By auditing event data and implementing logic flags built to alert on de-authentication storm triggers.
flashcards.back_example: Syslog trace: AP-WIDS: Deauth flood signature on station MAC
flashcards.back_confusion: Don't confuse signature-based detection (matching known strings) with anomaly-based detection (mapping dynamic standard deviations).
flashcards.back_hook: Detection is looking for the fingerprint left behind by the threat.
